lessonPlan.title: Pride and Prejudice unit
lessonPlan.author: Jane Austen
essentialQuestions: What does Pride and Prejudice suggest about first impressions and prejudice?
What does Pride and Prejudice suggest about pride and self-knowledge?
What does Pride and Prejudice suggest about marriage and money?
What does Pride and Prejudice suggest about class and social mobility?
What does Pride and Prejudice suggest about women's limited choices?
objectives: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly and implicitly.
Determine themes and analyze their development over the course of the novel.
Analyze how characters, setting and point of view interact.
Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in the text.
Write arguments to support claims with clear reasons and relevant evidence.
lessonPlan.differentiation: Every prompt and quiz has five rigor levels; the app applies student override, then class standard, then the automatic level.

Weekly writing prompt at assigned rigor

wholeBookTest.title: Pride and Prejudice: whole-book test

items.prompt: Whom does Bingley dance with twice?

options: A legal limit passing property to a set heir

items.prompt: Who visits Netherfield to check on Jane?
options: Mrs. Bennet with Lydia and Kitty

items.prompt: Why did Collins come to Longbourn?
options: To choose a wife among the daughters

items.prompt: How does Jane respond to Wickham's story?
options: She refuses to think ill of either man

items.prompt: How does Collins explain why he wants to marry?
options: He lists reasons, including Lady Catherine's advice
He says he loves her passionately

items.prompt: Who distracts Collins after the refusal?

options: Mrs. Bennet's brother and his wife

items.prompt: Where does Elizabeth stop on the way to Hunsford?
Who dominates the conversation at Rosings?
Who draws Elizabeth into lively conversation?

options: Darcy saved a friend from an imprudent marriage

items.prompt: How does Darcy respond to the rejection?
Who goes to London to search?
How do Lydia and Wickham behave?
Where do Jane and Bingley eventually live?

answerKey.answer: A legal limit passing property to a set heir
Mrs. Bennet with Lydia and Kitty
To choose a wife among the daughters
She refuses to think ill of either man
He lists reasons, including Lady Catherine's advice
Mrs. Bennet's brother and his wife
Darcy saved a friend from an imprudent marriage

shortAnswer: Explain how first impressions and prejudice develops from the beginning of the novel to the end. Use two chapters.
Explain how pride and self-knowledge develops from the beginning of the novel to the end. Use two chapters.
Explain how marriage and money develops from the beginning of the novel to the end. Use two chapters.
wholeBookTest.essay: Choose one of the novel's central concerns (first impressions and prejudice, pride and self-knowledge, marriage and money, class and social mobility, women's limited choices) and argue how the ending reframes it.

middleSchool.label: Middle School
middleSchool.text: Write a five-paragraph essay explaining what Pride and Prejudice teaches about first impressions and prejudice. Use at least three quotations from different parts of the book.

highSchool.label: High School / Common Core
highSchool.text: Write an argumentative essay analyzing how Jane Austen develops first impressions and prejudice across Pride and Prejudice. Trace the idea through at least three chapters and address a counterclaim.

ap.label: AP
ap.text: In a well-organized essay, analyze how Jane Austen uses a recurring literary element to shape the meaning of first impressions and prejudice in Pride and Prejudice. Do not merely summarize.

collegeFreshman.label: College Freshman
collegeFreshman.text: Write a researched essay (4–6 pages) that places Pride and Prejudice's treatment of first impressions and prejudice in its historical context, using at least two scholarly sources.

graduate.label: Graduate / PhD
graduate.text: Write a seminar paper (15–20 pages) that intervenes in the critical conversation on first impressions and prejudice in Pride and Prejudice, engaging the relevant scholarship and textual history.
